title: The Ethics of Tourism
description: A podcast episode asking whether travellers can be responsible: overcrowded destinations, volunteer trips, a local guide's view and the question of flying.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Podcast introduction
parts.intro: You will hear the hosts of a travel podcast, Mai and Jack, introducing today's topic.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Hello and welcome to Slow Roads, the podcast for people who have a nagging feeling about their last holiday. I'm Mai.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: And I'm Jack. Today's episode is about the ethics of tourism, which is a slightly awkward subject for two people who've spent most of their savings on travelling.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: It is. I'll start with a confession. Last summer, I went to a famous old harbour town that I'd dreamt of visiting for years. I arrived to find it had so many visitors that I couldn't actually see the harbour. I was standing in a queue to look at a wall.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: And you were, of course, part of the problem.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Exactly. That's the uncomfortable thing. Everyone complaining about overcrowding is also, by definition, a crowd. Residents in a number of cities have started to say that they can't afford to live in their own neighbourhoods because short-term holiday rentals have pushed rents up.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: To be fair, though, tourism pays wages. In some places it's the main source of income. If we all stopped going, whole communities would suffer.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Which is the dilemma in a nutshell. The question is not whether to travel, it's how, and how much.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: I'd add one more complication. Not all tourists are the same. A person who stays in a family guesthouse and eats at a local café spreads money differently from one who stays at a big resort that imports everything.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Right. So let's try to work out what actually helps.

parts.title: Part 2 · Volunteer tourism
parts.intro: You will hear Jack interviewing a researcher, Dr Okoye, about volunteer tourism.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Dr Okoye, you've studied what's called volunteer tourism, where travellers spend a week or two helping out in a developing country. It sounds wonderful. Is it?

script.speaker: Dr Okoye
script.text: In many cases, it's well intentioned and badly designed. The central problem is that these placements are usually built around what the visitor wants to experience, not around what the community needs.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Can you give an example?

script.speaker: Dr Okoye
script.text: Painting a school wall is a classic. A group of enthusiastic visitors pays a fee to paint a wall. Meanwhile, a local painter who could have done it in a day, and been paid, is left out. The visitors go home feeling good, and the community ends up slightly worse off.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: I've heard worse stories about orphanages.

script.speaker: Dr Okoye
script.text: Those are the most troubling. In some countries, the demand from visitors to hold and play with children has encouraged people to set up orphanages as businesses, and to recruit children who in fact have families. Children are separated from their parents so that tourists can feel useful. Sadly, there's good evidence for this.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: That's shocking. So should people simply stay at home?

script.speaker: Dr Okoye
script.text: No, I'm not saying that. I'd ask people to start with a different question. Instead of, how can I help, ask, what skills do I have that this community has asked for? A qualified nurse working under a local clinic's direction is a different thing altogether from an untrained teenager teaching English for a fortnight.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: So the key is that the community leads.

script.speaker: Dr Okoye
script.text: Yes. And a longer stay helps. Short visits create a lot of administrative work for the hosts, and they rarely leave anything lasting.

parts.title: Part 3 · A local voice
parts.intro: You will hear Mai speaking to Kwame, a guide who lives on a small island popular with visitors.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Kwame, you've been a guide on your island for twenty years. How has tourism changed it?

script.speaker: Kwame
script.text: Enormously. When I started, perhaps a few hundred people came each summer, and they stayed with families. Now we have cruise ships, and thousands arrive for six hours, and then they leave.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: That doesn't sound so bad. Surely they spend money?

script.speaker: Kwame
script.text: Less than you'd think. Many of them have eaten on the ship, and they've already bought their excursion from the cruise company. They walk through the town, take photographs, buy a magnet perhaps. Meanwhile, we have to repair the paths, collect the rubbish and supply water. The costs are ours, but the profits mostly aren't.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: What do residents think?

script.speaker: Kwame
script.text: It's divided. Some people have opened shops and they're grateful. Others, particularly the older ones, feel that the island has become a stage set. They say, we don't recognise our own streets. One friend refuses to go into the square between ten and four.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Is anything being done?

script.speaker: Kwame
script.text: The council has started limiting the number of ships per day, which has helped. And a group of us have begun offering small walks led by residents. Visitors hear real stories, we're paid properly and the groups are small enough not to disturb anyone.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: So what would you say to a traveller?

script.speaker: Kwame
script.text: Stay overnight, if you can. That's the single biggest thing. Someone who sleeps here eats here, drinks here and talks to us. And please, ask before photographing people. We're not part of the scenery.

parts.title: Part 4 · The flying question
parts.intro: You will hear Mai and Jack discussing flying and personal responsibility at the end of the episode.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: We can't end this without mentioning flying. Aviation is a large contributor to climate change, and for most of us, one long-haul flight produces more emissions than months of driving.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Which makes me squirm, because I love going to far-off places. I've heard the argument that individual choices don't matter, that it's up to governments and airlines.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: I find that argument too convenient. Governments respond to what citizens do and say. But I also think guilt is a poor motivator. People who feel judged tend to get defensive and do nothing.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: So what's your rule?

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Fewer trips, longer stays. Rather than three short breaks a year, take one proper trip, and go overland where it's practical. It's slower, but I've found the journey becomes part of the holiday.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: I'd add a modest suggestion. Be honest about your reasons. If you're flying to a city for a weekend simply because it's cheap, that's different from flying to see family you haven't met for years.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: That's a distinction I like. Not all journeys are equal.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: And if there's one idea I'd like listeners to take away, it's curiosity about consequences. Ask where your money goes, who benefits and who bears the cost. You won't always get a clean answer, but the asking changes how you travel.

script.speaker: Jack
script.text: Well said. Next week, we're heading to the mountains. Until then, travel thoughtfully.

questions.text: What was Mai's problem when she visited the harbour town?
options: She could not find a hotel near the harbour.
It was so crowded that she could not see it.
The weather was too poor to see the harbour.

evidence.quote: it had so many visitors that I couldn't actually see the harbour

Sure that she is not responsible

What skills do I have that locals asked for?
